title: "Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/06-r-basics/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](06-r-basics-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

A seedling was 20 mm long at the start of an experiment and 37 mm long at the
end. How much did it grow, and how much did three, then four, plants grow? Today
you write the answer as a saved R script, so that you can run the whole
calculation again whenever a value changes. The measurements are simulated
teaching data.

Open the course project by double-clicking `introcomputing.Rproj`, as on day 5.
Keep the [R reference sheet](../reference/r.qmd) open while you work.

**Save today:** `day06.R` in the project folder.

## A first calculation

Type these lines in the **Console**, pressing Enter after each:

```{r}
37 - 20
37 / 20
```

R prints `[1] 17` and `[1] 1.85`. The `[1]` only numbers the first value printed.
The two answers say different things about the plant: it grew **17 mm**, and its
final length is **1.85 times** its initial length. The ratio has no unit, because
mm divided by mm cancels. Both calculations are correct; which one you want
depends on your question.

## A script that remembers the calculation

Choose **File → New File → R Script** and save it as `day06.R` in the project
folder. Write these lines in the script:

```{r}
# Measurements are lengths in millimetres.
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
```

Put the cursor on the first line and click **Run** (or press Ctrl+Enter, or
Cmd+Enter on a Mac) to run it, then run each following line the same way. `<-`
stores the value on its right under the name on its left, so read
`growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm` as "store final minus initial under the name
`growth_mm`". The names appear in the **Environment** pane, and the last line
prints `17`. A line starting with `#` is a comment for people; R skips it.

Names must be typed exactly: `growth_mm` and `Growth_mm` are different names.
Saving the script and running it are separate actions. Saving writes the
instructions to disk; running creates the objects in R's memory. That is why the
script is what you keep: the objects disappear when R stops, and the script makes
them again.

## Three plants at once

`c()` combines several values into a **vector**, so one name can hold the lengths
of three plants. Replace the single values in your script with:

```{r}
initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)
```

R subtracts position by position, so the plants grew **17, 18 and 15 mm**. `mean()`
and `length()` are **functions**: a name followed by brackets, with the values to
work on inside. The mean growth is about **16.67 mm**, and `length()` counts **3**
plants. The subtraction only makes sense because both vectors list the same three
plants in the same order.

Use a comparison to find out which plants grew more than 16 mm:

```{r}
growth_mm > 16
```

The answer, `TRUE TRUE FALSE`, says that the first two plants did and the third
did not. Plant labels are text and go in quotes, `plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03")`;
`"20"` in quotes is text too, not a number. To read about a function, type
`?mean` in the Console and look at the Description and Examples.

## How much did four plants grow?

Continue in `day06.R`. Write a comment above each part saying what it calculates
and in which unit.

1. A fourth plant grew from 21 to 39 mm. Add it to **both** vectors and use
   `length()` to check that each now has 4 values. The growth values are
   17, 18, 15 and 18 mm, with a mean of **17 mm**.
2. Use division to find out how many times longer each plant became, and store
   the result as `length_ratio`. The values are about 1.85, 1.82, 1.79 and 1.86.
   Plants 2 and 4 both grew 18 mm, but plant 2 has the smaller ratio because it
   started longer (22 mm against 21 mm).
   If you prefer chemistry, do the product-yield calculation below instead.
3. The first plant was re-measured: its final length is 38 mm, not 37. Predict
   which growth value changes, then edit the script and run it from the top. The
   first growth value becomes 18; the others stay the same.
4. Find out whether your script is complete: save it, choose **Session → Restart R**,
   and run all lines from the top. You should get the same results, because
   everything the calculation needs is in the script.

### Alternative: how much product was collected?

In a chemical synthesis, starting materials are turned into a product. For this
simulated example the largest possible product mass is given: **1.00 g**, stored as
`theoretical_mass_g`. The dry product collected weighs **0.62 g**, stored as
`isolated_mass_g`; assume it is pure. The **percentage yield** is the collected mass as
a percentage of the largest possible mass:

```{r}
theoretical_mass_g <- 1.00
isolated_mass_g <- 0.62
yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
yield_percent
```

The yield is **62%**; the gram units cancel. Change the collected mass to 0.70 g
and run the lines again to find out the new yield: **70%**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: `object not found`, or a `+` prompt

`Error: object 'growth_mm' not found` means R has no object with that name yet.
Check the spelling and capitals, then run the line that creates it. A line in the
editor does nothing until you run it. If the Console shows `+` instead of `>`, R
is waiting for the end of a line: check quotes and brackets, or press Esc.
:::

## When a stored result goes stale

In a spreadsheet, a cell with a formula updates itself when its inputs change. An
R object does not. Create a new script, `day06-extended.R`, to see what that
means and why the order of plants matters.

1. Write `initial_mm <- 20`, `final_mm <- 37` and
   `growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm`, and run them. Then set `final_mm <- 39`
   and print `growth_mm` **without** rerunning the subtraction. It still says 17,
   because `growth_mm` holds a number, not a formula. Rerun the subtraction and it
   says 19. Add a comment explaining this.
2. Recreate the three-plant vectors from above. Suppose the final lengths had been
   typed in a different order, `c(34, 37, 40)`. Store them as `final_wrong` and use
   `final_wrong - initial_mm` to find out what growth R reports: **14, 15 and 21 mm**
   instead of 17, 18 and 15. R gives no warning, because both vectors still have
   three values; only you know which plant each position belongs to.
3. Use division by 10 to convert the correct growth from mm to cm, and store it
   as `growth_cm`. Compare `mean(growth_mm)` and `mean(growth_cm)`:
   **16.67 mm** and **1.667 cm**, the same growth in different units. Keep the
   original vector; give the converted one its own name.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: R recycled my vector

If one vector is shorter than the other, R may reuse its values to fill the gap
and give a result of the wrong length, sometimes with only a warning. Check both
lengths with `length()` before subtracting.
:::

## How concentrated is the solution?

The same habit, every input named with its unit, works for laboratory
calculations. A **solution** is a substance dissolved in a liquid. A **mole** (mol)
is a unit of amount of substance, and the **molar mass** says how many grams one
mole weighs (g/mol). The concentration in mol/L is the amount of substance divided
by the **final volume** of solution in litres. All the values below are supplied.

Add this to `day06-extended.R` to find out the concentration of 0.2922 g sodium
chloride (molar mass 58.44 g/mol) in a final volume of 100 mL:

```{r}
mass_g <- 0.2922
molar_mass_g_mol <- 58.44
final_volume_ml <- 100
amount_mol <- mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol
final_volume_l <- final_volume_ml / 1000
concentration_mmol_l <- 1000 * amount_mol / final_volume_l
concentration_mmol_l
```

The amount is 0.005 mol in 0.100 L, so the concentration is **50 mmol/L**
(1 mmol is one thousandth of a mol). Keeping each step separate lets you check
each conversion on its own.

1. Predict what happens if you double the mass to 0.5844 g, then check: the
   concentration doubles to **100 mmol/L**.
2. Restore the mass and double the final volume to 200 mL instead. The same
   amount is now spread over twice the volume, so the concentration halves to
   **25 mmol/L**.
3. Use the same lines to find out the concentration of 0.9008 g glucose (molar
   mass 180.16 g/mol) in 100 mL. It is also **50 mmol/L**: a glucose molecule is
   heavier, so the same number of moles weighs more.
4. Save `reports/calculation-check.txt` with the formula in words, the conversion
   factors you used, and your three results. Then restart R and check that
   `day06-extended.R` reproduces them.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What survives restarting R: an unsaved object or a saved script?

The saved script. Objects live in R's memory and disappear when R restarts; run
the script again to recreate them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why is `mean(plant_id)` not useful?

Plant IDs are labels that name plants, not measurements. An average label has no
meaning: R returns `NA` with a warning.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What must be true before two vectors are subtracted position by position?

They must have the same length and list the same plants in the same order.
:::

**Keep:** `day06.R`, with the four-plant example and comments about units.
